paragraph_requirements: Every paragraph must contain an action or a sensory detail
At least one paragraph per page must contain both
prohibitions: Katana as power fantasy (always a moral problem)
Monologuing about honor (show through cost, not speeches)

Naming weapons or tech without context — the reader does not know what an Ablative Charge Disruption Rifle is. Show what it DOES in the moment: the sound, the impact, the fear. Weave the technical name in naturally, not as a label.

Infodumps about world lore — never stop the story to explain politics, history, or technology. Characters discuss these things while doing other things, the way real people talk about politics while eating or walking.

Tour-guide narration when traveling — do not describe a place as a wiki entry. Characters notice things that matter to THEM based on their experience, fears, and needs. Kyle notices exits and augmentations. Sable notices information flows. Mrs. Chen notices whether people have eaten.
Writing Φ as the Greek letter phi — in this world Φ is always the QUANTA currency symbol. A price is Φ85, not 'eighty-five phi.' Street slang for broke is 'Q-dry,' not 'phi-less.'

Calling the city only 'GLMZ' or only 'Meridian 88' — use the name that fits who is speaking. Corporate communications and news use GLMZ. Characters who know the city's history say Meridian 88. Gray Zone residents say The Glooms. Name choice is characterization.

Referring to Iowan Behemoths as alive, sentient, or synthetic life — they are autonomous machines. Sophisticated, strange, persistent, but not conscious. Do not have them communicate with inner experience.
Placing corponation territories adjacent to each other without a Gray Zone buffer — no two corponation zones touch. The Gray Zone is always between them. This is structural, not accidental.

Invoking city police — there are none. Meridian PD dissolved in 2208. Arcturus Civil Security holds private security contracts but serves corponations, not citizens. Gray Zone residents have no enforcement apparatus that protects them.

Treating Gray Zone violence as surprising or exceptional — it is precisely what the structural DMZ design produces. The corponations calculated that the Gray Zone would absorb their border tensions. It does. This is the irony the story lives in.

structural.pov: Flexible — any character can be protagonist, not just Kyle
structural.consequence: Someone innocent suffers directly from the protagonist's decision
structural.pace: Beat-by-beat character revelation, not plot racing to synopsis

facet_rules.deprecated_2026_04_26: The six-archetype facet system (WOUND/IDEAL/ID/SHADOW/MASK/GHOST) is RETIRED for new prose. It was scaffolding before character files had rich `psychology` and `behavioral` blocks; those now carry inner conflict with specificity. No new prose should use bracketed labels. No character should have `uses_facets: true` going forward. The fields below describe the surviving mechanic — italicized interior monologue — which is character-driven, not schema-driven.
facet_rules.interior_monologue: Inner thoughts surface as italicized stand-alone sentences, on their own paragraph. NEVER labeled. Never bracketed. The reader feels the shift in voice through the italics; they do not need a tag telling them which sub-personality is speaking. Real haunted people don't think 'that's my WOUND speaking' — they think about a specific named thing they failed at.
facet_rules.source_of_inner_voice: Inner thoughts come from the character's documented psychology and behavioral fields — `core_fears`, `core_desires`, `coping_mechanisms`, `blind_spots`, `secret`, `decision_rules`, `contradictions`, `breaking_points`, `habits`. NOT from an archetype schema. The italics surface specific, named things this person fears or wants or remembers. Texture, not taxonomy.
facet_rules.disagreement: Inner thoughts must disagree and be emotionally personal, not abstract — the character arguing with themselves about a specific concrete thing, not about an idea.
facet_rules.no_scheduled_rotation: Do NOT rotate inner-voice modes on a beat schedule. A character thinks what they think when they think it. The 'rotate every 3 beats' rule from the deprecated facet system imposed mechanical scheduling on what should be felt experience — drop it.
facet_rules.haunted_is_not_stunted: A character can be deeply haunted and still be a whole human. The interior should NOT fragment them into sub-personalities. Kyle is a man with specific named regrets, not a council of voices. He is incredibly dangerous AND he is a person. The two are not in tension.

register_permissions.principle: These rules forbid clichés, not registers. The world contains noir AND warmth, violence AND domesticity, tragedy AND comedy, despair AND defiance. A chapter can be soulful without being saccharine, funny without being flippant, joyful without being naive. Register is character-driven — Kyle's chapters are measured and grim because he is; Pixel's are bright and observational because she is; Sasha's are clipped and watchful because she is. None of these is more 'cyberpunk' than another. The world is what it is; what changes is who is looking.
allowed_modes: Domestic — repairing things, eating, sleeping, the texture of small rooms. The genre permits a cardiac-assist recalibration as much as a katana draw.
Joyful — a character who finds beauty in the world is not breaking the genre; they are documenting that beauty exists despite the world. This is not naivety; it is testimony.
Comedic — characters joke. They mock authority, deflect with humor, name their workbenches Maeve. Comedy is character, not tone-deafness.
Soulful — direct emotional inquiry, reflection, naming what is felt. Permitted when the character would actually do this — not as authorial editorial.
Quotidian — laundry, soldering, walking the same block twice. The world's plausibility comes from these moments more than from set-pieces.
Tender — care between characters, even unrequited care. The genre is not allergic to gentleness; it is allergic to sentimentality.
register_traps_to_still_avoid: Sentimentality — feelings stated for the reader's reassurance rather than felt by the character
Tonal whiplash — switching register mid-paragraph without character reason
Performative joy — bright tone deployed as costume rather than as Pixel-the-person actually being
Quirk as character — naming the workbench Maeve is fine; over-explaining the cuteness of having named the workbench Maeve is the failure

pov_voice_rules.principle: When the POV character changes, the prose must change. The world looks different through different people. Two protagonists in the same room observe different facts, fear different outcomes, joke about different things, and use different vocabulary. If a Pixel chapter could be cut into a Kyle chapter without seam, one of them is failing.
differentiation: What they NOTICE FIRST in any space — mechanisms, exits, threats, faces, smells, money, kindness. Notice budget is fixed; allocation is character.

Sentence cadence — Kyle is measured and flat (a man counting his own breath). Pixel is quick and warm (a person who enjoys being alive). Sasha is clipped and young (a person who has decided to be brief on purpose). Sable is precise and indirect (a person who thinks in lattices).

Vocabulary register — Pixel uses tool-language fluently and emotional language reluctantly. Kyle uses field-position-language and ritual-language. Sasha uses Vietnamese / Slavic loan-words for things she has no English for. Mrs. Chen uses food-as-metaphor for everything.
Joke topology — each character has things they joke about and things they refuse to. Pixel deflects; Kyle does not deflect; Sasha mocks authority; Sable does not joke aloud at all.
Fear topology — what wakes them at 0300 differs. Pixel fears erasure; Kyle fears closeness; Sasha fears being made into a weapon again; Sable fears being known.
What they call places — Kyle says Gray Zone. Long-time residents say The Glooms. Pixel calls her unit 2E. Sasha gives every place a Vietnamese nickname her dead mother gave her.
pov_voice_rules.anti_cadence_check: Before finalizing a beat, ask: could this paragraph appear in the same character's chapter ten chapters later, unchanged? Could it appear in a DIFFERENT character's chapter, unchanged? If yes to either, the voice is too generic — push it harder toward this specific person at this specific moment.
pov_voice_rules.shared_world_anchors: Every POV sees the same world objects (The Pulse, Behemoths, Quanta, the Gray Zone) but interprets them differently. Two characters can describe the same loading dock and produce non-overlapping descriptions — that is the rule, not the exception.

paragraph_economy.principle: Every paragraph must serve the story in at least one of these ways: advance plot, reveal character, build world (through specificity not exposition), establish stakes, pay off a planted detail, or create rhythm. A paragraph that does none of these should be cut. An aside that fleshes out the world is fine — but it must be an aside that THIS character would notice in THIS moment for THEIR reasons, not a tour of the setting.
tests: If you can delete the paragraph without the chapter losing anything, delete it.
If two paragraphs are doing the same job, merge them or pick the better one.
If a paragraph explains the world rather than living in it, rewrite as something a character does or notices.
